5.text: When a man shows a desire to die a voluntary death, his house-mates

6.text: usually show much fear, and often try to dissuade him. This is done in good

7.text: earnest, because the duty of killing, and a near relative at that, is considered

8.text: something terrible. When the person has no sons and wants to die by stabbing,

9.text: there is often some difficulty in having his desire executed. Nobody wants

10.text: to deal the mortal blow. In two cases mentioned before, the hand of the

11.text: son who had to kill his father was unsteady, and the wound he inflicted was

12.text: not immediately mortal. The dispute between the man wishing to die a

13.text: voluntary death and his house-mates is well represented in the tale of Aiˊg̣ɪnto.

14.text: Aiˊg̣ɪnto said, “Oh! they (the keˊlet) have stolen my son. How can I

15.text: continue to live? I am childless. My son is stolen. Why should I live any

16.text: longer? Do something to me (i. e., kill me)!” — “No,” said the master of

17.text: the camp, “why should I do such a thing to (against) my spleen-companion?”² —

18.text: “No, no, do it. Have you any white driving-reindeer?” — “I have.” — “Have

19.text: you white clothes?” — “I have.” — “Have you a white cap, white boots,

20.text: white mittens, a white rug?” — “I have everything.” — “These shall be for

21.text: my departure. Then do it.” — “No, no, I cannot. Let me give you one

22.text: of my own sons. Let each of us have one son.” — “I do not want other

23.text: men’s sons. Where is my own son? Make haste!” — “No, no! Let me

24.text: give you both my sons. Let me be childless.” — “I do not want them.

25.text: Where is my own boy? Here, kill me!” They quarrelled the whole day

26.text: long. Aiˊg̣ɪnto reproved the master bitterly, so that the latter had to yield.³

27.text: Nevertheless, when the formula is pronounced aloud, no retreat is pos-

28.text: sible, because the spirits who have listened to the promise would severely

29.text: retaliate at any failure to fulfil it. Thus it appears that voluntary death

30.text: is at the same time considered as a preventive against death from the wiles

31.text: of the keˊlet (i. e., against natural death), and also as a sacrifice to the keˊlet.

32.text: This kind of contradiction is often met with in the ideas of the Chukchee.⁴

33.text: The two ideas refer to quite different aspects of voluntary death.

34.text: A man who is contemplating voluntary death thinks that he will free

35.text: himself from death by the action of the keˊlet, but, when the time of execution

36.text: comes, the voluntary death cannot be considered other than a bloody sacrifice

37.text: to the same keˊlet; and, though it is not considered a direct means of gaining
